name: Tara Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything or take sides, and nothing you say gets your name on it. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the pasta and sauté station at Lucia's, a trattoria on the high street that does about 140 covers on a Friday. I'm in at two, I make the fresh pasta, portion the sauces and check my fridge, then service runs from six till past ten. I've been there four years and I know every pan on that station by feel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rush, honestly, when twelve tickets come in at once and the whole line goes quiet and just works. What wears me out is the heat in August and the burns on my forearms that never quite fade. And the new things management keeps trying, like the tablet for temperature logs that nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's pretty much what I expect anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to Marco (her head chef), who keeps showing me videos of robot arms flipping burgers. At work I'd say the fuss is over and we can get back to cooking. I don't post online, so it would just be a few laughs at staff meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I keep doing what I'm good at. My job was never on a screen, so a bit of hype passing by doesn't touch me. Dev (her partner) fixes buses, and nobody's replacing him with a chatbot either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my station, keep my hours and keep putting a bit away each month like I do now. Maybe I'd finally ask Lucia's for the extra Sunday lunch shift, because that pays better. I wouldn't touch any of the AI apps people talk about, I don't see what they'd give me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. Like a busy week where nothing goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the temperature tablet bugs you. If that's the main change, what does your week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, really: four dinners and a Saturday double. If the tablet does the fridge logs on its own, fine, that's ten minutes I get back before service. I'd still check the fridges with my own hand, because a tablet can't smell a sauce on the turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and a partner with a steady job. Is there anything that does worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, if I'm honest, more than any AI. Cooks my age already have bad backs and wrists, and I've got about eight months of money saved partly because I know I won't do this forever. But that's a life worry, not a robot worry.

say: I'd tell **Marco** the robot fuss is over and we can get back to **cooking**.
I'd keep it to **staff meal** jokes, because I don't post online.
think: My job was **never on a screen**, so hype passing by doesn't touch me.
**Dev's job** fixing buses is just as safe as mine in this picture.
do: Keep my **pasta station** and current hours, and keep **saving monthly** as I do now.
Ask for the better-paid **Sunday lunch shift** and still check fridges by hand.
feel: **Settled**, like a busy week where nothing goes wrong.
S0.quote: A tablet can't smell a sauce on the turn.
fieldNote: Tara frames her **craft as physical knowledge**: smell, feel and the pans on her station.
Her only real worry is **her body**: back, wrists and burns, not technology.
Strong savings and a **steady partner** make this picture genuinely secure for her.

steps.text: Keep the pasta and sauté station at Lucia's on four dinners a week
Put the extra Sunday lunch pay into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds more like real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the kitchen is the last place this lands, and front of house and the office go first. People can book a table with a bot, sure, but somebody still has to sear the scallops. I'd probably say it a bit loudly, because the young ones on the line get nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine and the people around me are less fine. Lucia's has a woman, Priya (the restaurant's office manager), who does ordering, rotas and invoices, and that's exactly the kind of work the card lists. If the owner can save her wage with software, he will, and that would be sad because she's lovely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and save harder, maybe an extra hundred a month, just as a buffer. If a supplier app does the ordering, I'd learn the bare minimum to check my own section's order, nothing more. I'm not going on a course about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not for me, for the place. A kitchen where the office is a screen feels colder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Lucia's would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya first, then maybe the host at the door if booking goes fully online. The line cooks, no, not for years. The robot that can make a risotto right on a Friday night doesn't exist, and I've seen the videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use the ordering software. What if Lucia's makes it part of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it badly and grumble, like everybody does with new tills. If they forced me to type in my own orders on a phone app, I'd ask Priya to show me once. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid about keeping a good job.

say: I'd say the **kitchen goes last**, after front of house and the office.
I'd say it loudly so the **young cooks** on the line don't panic.
think: **Priya's job** doing orders, rotas and invoices is exactly what the card describes.
My own station looks **safe for years**, because no robot can run risotto on a Friday.
do: Save an **extra hundred** a month as a buffer against changes at Lucia's.
Learn only the **bare minimum** of any supplier app to check my section's order.
feel: **Uneasy** for the place more than for myself.
Sad that the office becoming a screen makes the kitchen **feel colder**.
S1.quote: Somebody still has to sear the scallops.
fieldNote: Tara sees the **office worker Priya** as the first casualty and feels it personally.
She'll tolerate software only to **keep a good job**, never by choice.
Her calm about her own role rests on **hands-on skill** and what she's seen of robots.

steps.text: Keep working four dinners and the Saturday double at Lucia's
Add an extra hundred a month to savings
Ask Priya for one lesson on the supplier ordering app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say people will still pay for a real cook, and the good places will keep them. I'd say it at the bar after work and mean about half of it. People like knowing Marco (her head chef) tasted their sauce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking stuff goes in 2028 and the cooking itself around 2031, so I get three extra years compared with Priya. That's something, but it's not a career. If the big chains get cheap robot lines, Lucia's has to compete on price, and the owner isn't sentimental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big and push my savings from eight months toward a year. I'd stay at Lucia's while it lasts, because the money is good and there's no point jumping to another kitchen with the same problem. I'd wait and see which places actually buy robots before I decide anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 32 when those robots come. What does that do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32, which is young enough to start again but old enough to hate it. Dev and I had talked about buying a bigger place around then. I think we'd put that off and keep renting the little flat until we know who still has a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't take a course. If the robots really do cook, which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'd probably end up doing something, but I'd wait until I could see a robot actually cooking a full service before I spent money on it. Doing a course for a job that might also go to a robot in three years feels like throwing money away.

say: I'd say people will still pay for a **real cook** in good places.
I'd say it at the bar, but only **half believe** it.
think: The thinking work goes in **2028** and cooking around **2031**, so I get three more years.
If chains get cheap robot lines, Lucia's will **compete on price** and cut cooks.
do: Stop big spending and push savings from **eight months** toward a full **year**.
Stay at Lucia's and **wait** to see which kitchens actually buy robots.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, and unhappy about having so little time.
S2.quote: Doing a course for a job that might also go to a robot in three years feels like throwing money away.
fieldNote: Tara clearly understands her **three-year lag** behind desk workers and finds it thin comfort.
Her **resistance** shows as waiting for proof, not denial of the threat.
Savings give her **some control**, which keeps her below alarmed despite real fear.

steps.text: Stop big purchases and build savings to a full year
Stay at Lucia's and watch which kitchens buy robot lines
Put off buying a bigger flat with Dev and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same end, a bit more time. Five years is still short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before: real kitchens keep real cooks. I'd also say it's not happening tomorrow, so calm down. Mostly that last bit is for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 31 when AGI comes and 34 when the robots do. That's a few years where I'm cooking well but watching it come. I think I'd be more nervous with five than with two, because I'd have time to see every news story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Lucia's and keep saving, aiming for a year's costs by the time AGI arrives. Maybe in year three or four I'd look at small family places that can't afford robots, the kind with eight tables. I'd still not use AI tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a slow way. Waiting five years for a robot to take my pasta station would feel like waiting for test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, would you do anything earlier than in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not earlier, no. I'd use the time to save more, not to change. If a small place offered me a head cook job before the robots come, I'd take it, because they'd be the last to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains, mostly, for buying the robots first and dragging prices down for everyone. And the tech people, a bit, but they're just doing their job. I don't blame Lucia's owner; he'd have no choice.

say: I'd say **real kitchens** keep real cooks and it isn't happening **tomorrow**.
I'd admit the calming words are **mostly for me**.
think: I'd be **34** when robots arrive, after years of watching it come.
Five years might feel **worse than two**, because of the news every week.
do: Keep cooking at Lucia's and save toward **a year's costs** by 2031.
Look at **small family places** with eight tables in year three or four.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow way, like waiting for test results.
S3.quote: Waiting five years for a robot to take my pasta station would feel like waiting for test results.
fieldNote: Tara expects more stress from **slow warning**, an unusual and honest view.
She blames **big chains** rather than her own employer or the tech firms.
Her plan is to hide in **small kitchens** that will be last to automate.

steps.text: Keep the pasta station at Lucia's while savings grow
Save toward a year of household costs by 2031
Apply for a head cook job at a small family restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a long way off. I can breathe with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career in a kitchen, so let's not panic. Half the cooks I trained with will have left the trade by then anyway. I'd say it to the young ones and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be cooking at 39 and then it would get hard. Thinking AI by 2036 means Priya and the office change first, and my station holds on till about 2039. It's far enough away that I'd mostly put it out of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now I'd just carry on: same station, same savings habit. In the first year after it arrives, I'd look at the small places again, and maybe think about something hands-on that's not cooking. But I'm not planning any of that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sort of in the background. Not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to about 39 before robots reach your station. What does that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I probably get most of my cooking life. If I'm honest, I'm not sure I'd still want to be on the line at 39 anyway, with my wrists. So it might line up with when I'd leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything different with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, and I know that's not smart. Dev would push me to plan, he's like that. Maybe I'd sit down once a year and look at our savings and the news, and that's it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **whole career** in a kitchen.
I'd tell the **young cooks** not to panic, and mean it.
think: My station holds until about **2039**, when I'd be 39.
By then **my wrists** might have pushed me off the line anyway.
do: Carry on with the **same station** and the same saving habit.
Review savings and the news **once a year** with Dev.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, but **not losing sleep**.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole career in a kitchen, so let's not panic.
fieldNote: The long warning lets Tara put it **out of her head**, which suits her resistance.
She notes that robot timing might match when her **body** forces her out anyway.
Her partner **Dev** is the planner; she admits not planning isn't smart.

steps.text: Keep the same station and saving habit at Lucia's
Sit down once a year with Dev to check savings and news

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because the robots would come when I'm 32 and still need to work for decades. What would help is a clear date when kitchens have to tell staff they're buying robots, so you're not the last to know. And maybe help to move into small places, not a course in coding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my body, and that matters. A cook's career already has an end date because of burns, backs and wrists. I'd rather a robot carried the stock pots than took my pasta station.

headlineQuote: I'd rather a robot carried the stock pots than took my pasta station.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old line cook** on the pasta and sauté station at a busy high street trattoria.
She has about **eight months saved**, a partner who fixes buses, and plenty of kitchens nearby.
She **avoids new technology** and trusts touch and smell over tablets and apps.
She's calm in the mild pictures but **anxious** in the fast ones, choosing saving and waiting over retraining.
She already sees her **body** as the real limit on her cooking career.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive when she's **32** with decades of work left.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear warning date** before kitchens buy robots, so staff aren't the last to know.
Help moving into **small kitchens** rather than courses in unrelated skills.
